transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Well, I'm here because I just can't stop thinking that the left side of my face looks crooked. It just looks really messed up to me. It's constantly on my mind, and I feel like everyone at the warehouse where I work is noticing it. Even when I try to do things I enjoy, like going to salsa night, I just know people are staring at it. They tell me they don't see anything wrong when I ask, but... I just can't shake it. It's really getting to me.
Do you find yourself checking your face in mirrors, taking photos of it, or asking others repeatedly if they notice anything wrong with how it looks?

Yeah, I do. At work, especially. Like... before I go back out on the inventory floor, I just keep checking my face in the bathroom mirror. I'll stand there fixing my cap, trying to see how it looks, and just rubbing at that same spot on my face over and over. 

It gets pretty bad because sometimes I'm in there so long that I'm late getting back out to my section. My picking numbers fall behind because of it, and my boss has been getting on me again about my times. So, yeah, I do check it a lot.
Besides the way your face looks, do you experience any physical sensations in that area—like pain, tingling, numbness, or weakness?
No, I don't feel anything like that. It doesn't hurt or tingle or anything. It feels totally normal... it's just the way it looks that's the problem.

The patient's preoccupation is focused on a specific perceived physical defect (facial asymmetry) with repetitive mirror checking and reassurance-seeking, coupled with significant functional impairment. This is highly characteristic of Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.4). The absence of physical sensations and the purely perceptual/appearance-based concern further supports F45.4 over nonspecific neurotic presentations.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD), characterized by preoccupation with a perceived defect in facial appearance (left side of face appearing crooked) that is not observable or appears slight to others. The preoccupation causes clinically significant distress and functional impairment (decreased work productivity, avoidance of social activities). Repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, face rubbing, repeated reassurance-seeking) are present. The concern is focused on appearance rather than physical symptoms, ruling out somatic symptom disorder.

confirmed_symptoms: Persistent preoccupation with perceived defect in left side of face (crooked appearance)
Patient perceives significant appearance flaw that others do not observe or see as minimal
Intrusive thoughts about facial appearance ('constantly on my mind')
Belief that others are noticing the perceived defect despite reassurance to the contrary
Frequent mirror checking in bathroom before returning to work
Repeated touching/rubbing of the same spot on face
Repeated reassurance-seeking from coworkers about appearance
Clinically significant distress ('really getting to me')
Functional impairment at work (decreased picking productivity, tardiness)
Avoidance of social activities (hesitation about salsa night due to appearance concerns)
No physical pain, tingling, numbness, or weakness in affected area

additional_requirements: Preoccupation not better explained by concerns with body fat or weight (as in eating disorder)
Preoccupation not attributable to appearance concerns in context of gender dysphoria
